submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires when text reports or attributes a statement — it is a reported-speech/reported-writing detector. It is active on a reporting verb or noun (said, says, told, wrote, writes, remarked, noted, stated, explained, declared, added, replied, announced, confirmed, reported, 'according to', statement, letter, report) and peaks on the token that carries the attribution: the comma, colon or full stop that closes the reporting clause, the connector that opens the reported content ('that', 'how', 'whether', 'on', 'about', 'of', 'for', 'regarding', 'to'), a source or date inside the attribution ('said on Sunday', 'told The Washington Post Friday'), or the first words of the reported clause. The same punctuation, dates and connectors outside an attribution stay inactive: a plain date ('We went to the beach on Sunday'), 'that' after a non-reporting predicate ('the fact that', 'she noticed that', 'the analyst believed that', 'the court ruled that'), or a comma in an ordinary clause.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The city council voted 7 to 2 on Tuesday night to approve a rezoning plan that would allow developers to build as many as four thousand apartments on the site of the old rail yard, ending a debate that had dragged on for nearly three years. Supporters argued that the project would bring thousands of construction jobs and much-needed housing to a neighborhood where rents have climbed faster than anywhere else in the region. Critics, who packed the chamber hours before the meeting began, warned that the plan would overwhelm the district's schools and its water system, and that traffic on the surrounding streets would become unbearable.

The mayor, who had stayed out of the fight until the final week, cast the deciding vote after a short statement from his office. Speaking to reporters outside City Hall on Wednesday morning, the council's chief planner, Elena Ruiz, said that construction could begin as early as next spring, depending on the outcome of two environmental reviews. 'We have been waiting for this decision for a very long time,' she added. 'The site has sat empty for a generation, and the families who live nearby deserve to see something happen there.'

Not everyone was convinced. The head of the local school board, Marcus Feld, said the district had been given no more than a rough estimate of how many children would arrive, and that the money promised for a new elementary school had not yet appeared in any budget document. 'We are being asked to plan around a promise,' he said. 'That is not the same as a plan.' City officials responded that the first phase of the development would include a community center and a small park along the creek, and that a share of the tax revenue would be set aside for school construction.

The developer, a partnership between two firms based in the region, hopes to break ground before the end of the year, though the environmental reviews could push the timeline into the following summer. Opponents have promised to challenge the decision in court, arguing that the council failed to consider the cumulative effects of several other projects planned within a mile of the rail yard. A spokesperson for the opposition group said on Wednesday evening that the group had already retained a lawyer and expected to file within thirty days.

For the residents of the neighborhood, the vote was less an ending than the beginning of a long argument over what the site should become. Several of them lingered in the hallway afterward, trading predictions about how quickly the first buildings would rise and whether rents in the older blocks would climb even before the foundations were poured. One woman, who had lived in the same row house since the 1980s, said she had seen three plans for the rail yard come and go. 'Each time they tell us this is the one,' she said. 'Maybe this time they mean it.'

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The tide on the marsh arrives faster than it looks from the road, and on the first Saturday in May it caught three of us halfway across the mudflat, boots in hand, laughing at the cold. We had set out at six, when the light was still grey and the herons stood motionless in the shallows, and by seven the water had already begun to thread its way through the channels that the winter storms had cut into the bank. The plan was simple: cross to the island, count the nests along the eastern edge, and be back on the causeway before the water rose.

The island is small, about a quarter of a mile from end to end, with a low ridge along its spine and a stand of dead pines that the salt has slowly killed. On the day we went, the nests were fewer than the year before, though the grasses the birds use for cover had grown thick and tall. We marked each nest with a wooden stake, painted a number on the stake, and drew the positions onto a hand-drawn map. At the northern point we added a second row of stakes, since the dunes there had shifted a good ten feet since the previous survey.

By nine the wind had shifted, the water had climbed into the lower channels, and we decided to leave before the main creek became impassable. The walk back took about forty minutes, most of it through knee-deep water that was colder than either of us expected. My companion, who has studied these birds for two decades, kept a running count aloud, a habit of hers from years of working alone on the reserve. She carries a small notebook in her coat, a pencil stub in the binding, and a pair of binoculars that have been repaired twice with tape and wire.

There is a particular quiet on the marsh in early spring, before the boats return and the road crews begin their work on the causeway. The gulls take up the noise instead, and the wind through the dead pines makes a sound that is almost like a low whistle. We stopped once, halfway back, to watch a pair of oystercatchers work the edge of a channel, and then we kept going, because the tide was still rising and the causeway was the only way off the island that did not end in deep water. Next year, if the weather holds, we will start an hour earlier and bring a second thermos, and perhaps a rope.
